slides.title: Chapter 1: What Is Curvature?
slides.notes: Open the chapter by separating the word curvature from any single formula. The textbook uses the first pages to motivate the question rather than to compute, and our lecture mirrors that: we want students to feel why a quantitative notion of bending is needed before we define one. Tell students that by the end we will preview classification theorems and the local-to-global bridge that the rest of the book pays back.

slides.title: Three Surfaces, Three Curvatures
slides.notes: Use these three pictures as the textbook does on the opening pages. The plane is the calibrating example with zero curvature, the sphere shows uniform positive bending, and the saddle shows mixed bending whose product is negative. Insist that all three look locally like a piece of paper at first glance, so the curvature we are after must come from comparing nearby behaviour, not from a single tangent plane.

slides.title: Gaussian Curvature: An Intrinsic Number at a Point
slides.notes: Walk students through the construction in two stages. First, choose a normal direction and compare how the surface deviates from its tangent plane along each tangent direction; the extreme values are the principal curvatures. Second, take their product. The deep surprise that the chapter previews is the Theorema Egregium: this number can be recovered without ever leaving the surface, which is exactly why it deserves to be called intrinsic.

slides.title: How an Inhabitant Detects Curvature
slides.notes: This is the bridge from the abstract definition to something a student can imagine performing. Hand them a tiny triangle whose sides are geodesics and tell them to measure its three angles. On a sphere the sum is greater than pi; on a saddle it is less. This is the same data Gauss-Bonnet packages, and the chapter uses it to argue that curvature is not just a number but a measurable feature of intrinsic geometry.

slides.title: From Surfaces to Higher Dimensions: Sectional Curvature
slides.notes: Frame sectional curvature as the most economical generalization of Gaussian curvature. We pick a 2-plane inside the tangent space, run geodesics tangent to it, and read the Gaussian curvature of that surface. The Riemann tensor is just the bookkeeper that stores all of these numbers simultaneously. This is the abstraction the rest of the book will lean on.

slides.title: Classification: Constant Curvature Model Spaces
slides.notes: The classification results are the first big payoff of the curvature concept. Once you ask for constant sectional curvature and complete simply connected geometry, there are only three answers in each dimension. Use this as motivation: the rest of the book is in part the story of how local curvature data forces global shape, with these three models as the rigid endpoints.

slides.title: Local-to-Global Teasers
slides.notes: Preview Cartan-Hadamard and Bonnet-Myers as the two faces of the local-to-global story. Negative curvature lets geodesics spread, so the universal cover unfolds into Euclidean space. Positive Ricci curvature focuses geodesics, so the manifold cannot be larger than a sphere of comparable curvature. Students should leave this slide expecting the rest of the course to make these inequalities precise.

slides.title: The Chapter as a Dependency Map
slides.notes: Bring the notebook's concept graph into the lecture so students see the explicit anchors used in the reproducible material. The seven nodes mirror the chapter outline, and the central position of curvature is deliberate. Use this slide to remind students that motivation feeds classification, which in turn feeds local-to-global theorems that we will verify computationally later.

slides.title: The Computational Compass
slides.notes: Introduce these three formulas as the navigation tools for the rest of the course. Sectional curvature is the geometric object, Ricci curvature is the first useful contraction, and metric compatibility is the algebraic constraint that picks out the Levi-Civita connection. The notebook check is not a proof, but it gives students a place to perturb data and watch invariants respond.

slides.title: What This Chapter Hands Off
slides.notes: Close by reinforcing the three takeaways and giving students a habit for the rest of the book. Every new construction should be checked against the model spaces and read as a refinement of either the classification story or the local-to-global story. End with the diagnostic question so students arrive at chapter 2 already asking what role each new object plays.
